query: We are investigating the atomic-scale thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy alloy (HENA) nanoparticles synthesized via pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane. The prevailing hypothesis is that high entropy and sluggish diffusion stabilize the FCC structure against coalescence and segregation. However, in situ heating experiments reveal a progressive loss of sub-5 nm particles and a widening of the size distribution, alongside a reshaping from elliptical to spherical geometries. Theoretical models based on Gibbs free energy often neglect surface energy terms critical for sub-10 nm systems. It has been observed that the FCC structure in these PLD-grown NPs may be governed by kinetic effects rather than entropy. Propose a mechanism explaining why atomic diffusion is surprisingly active in this quinary system, leading to the segregation of specific elements (like Au and Cu) to the surface and subsequent evaporation. Identify the critical temperature threshold where this mechanism becomes dominant, establish the boundary conditions regarding the initial nanoparticle shape (icosahedral vs. truncated octahedron), and formulate a falsification experiment involving simultaneous in situ STEM and atomistic simulations to test if surface energy gradients alone can explain the observed phase separation without invoking sluggish diffusion.

generation.hypothesis: In sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles, the high surface-to-volume ratio causes the surface energy term ($\gamma$) to dominate the Gibbs free energy ($G = H - TS + \gamma A$), overriding the configurational entropy ($S_{conf}$) stabilization. Au and Cu, having significantly lower surface energies and higher vapor pressures compared to Co, Ni, and Pt, segregate to the surface to minimize total energy. This segregation creates a surface composition gradient that drives rapid atomic diffusion (contrary to the 'sluggish diffusion' hypothesis) because the driving force for surface segregation ($\Delta G_{seg}$) exceeds the activation barrier for diffusion at temperatures above a critical threshold. The reshaping from elliptical to spherical geometries is a direct consequence of minimizing surface area ($A$) to reduce surface energy. The critical temperature threshold ($T_{crit}$) is estimated to be approximately 400-500 K, where the thermal energy ($k_B T$) becomes sufficient to overcome the diffusion barriers for the segregated species, leading to evaporation of the surface-enriched Au and Cu. The initial shape (icosahedral vs. truncated octahedron) dictates the specific surface energy anisotropy; icosahedral particles with high surface energy facets will undergo faster reshaping and evaporation than truncated octahedra which are closer to the Wulff construction equilibrium shape.
generation.material_initial_state: Sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles, likely icosahedral or elliptical, synthesized via PLD on Si3N4, initially in a metastable FCC state stabilized by kinetic trapping.
generation.intervention: In situ heating in a transmission electron microscope (STEM) environment.
generation.conditions: Temperature ramp from room temperature to >600 K, vacuum or inert atmosphere, observation of size distribution and morphology changes.
generation.structural_mediator: Surface energy gradients and composition-dependent surface segregation of Au/Cu.
generation.mechanism: Derived from materials science principles: In sub-10 nm systems, the surface energy contribution ($\gamma A$) to the total free energy scales as $1/r$, while bulk entropy scales as constant. For AuCoCuNiPt, the surface energy of Au and Cu is significantly lower than Co, Ni, and Pt. To minimize total energy, Au and Cu segregate to the surface. This segregation creates a chemical potential gradient that drives rapid diffusion of these elements to the surface, bypassing the 'sluggish diffusion' typically observed in bulk HEAs where the driving force is lower. Once at the surface, the high vapor pressure of Au and Cu leads to evaporation, causing particle shrinkage and widening of the size distribution. The reshaping to spheres minimizes surface area. This mechanism is driven by surface thermodynamics rather than bulk entropy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Progressive loss of particle mass (shrinkage) and number density (evaporation of small particles) above 450 K. The size distribution will widen as smaller particles evaporate faster. The aspect ratio will decrease (elliptical to spherical). EDS mapping will show Au and Cu enrichment at the surface of remaining particles. The FCC structure may be retained or transform depending on the final composition, but the primary observation is mass loss and shape change.
generation.baseline: The prevailing hypothesis that high entropy and sluggish diffusion stabilize the FCC structure and prevent coalescence/segregation up to high temperatures.
generation.boundary: The mechanism is dominant for particle sizes < 10 nm. For particles > 50 nm, bulk entropy and sluggish diffusion should dominate, and the effect should be negligible. The effect is specific to alloys containing elements with large differences in surface energy and vapor pressure (like Au/Cu vs Pt/Co).
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical temperature ($T_{crit}$) is uncertain and depends on the specific initial composition and the exact surface energy values of the specific facets exposed. The rate of evaporation is highly sensitive to the local vacuum pressure and temperature ramp rate. The initial shape distribution (icosahedral vs truncated octahedron) introduces variability in the onset of reshaping.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform simultaneous in situ STEM heating and atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations on a model AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticle. The experiment will vary the initial shape (icosahedral vs truncated octahedron) and measure the rate of Au/Cu surface segregation and evaporation. The simulation will explicitly calculate the surface energy gradients and diffusion coefficients without assuming sluggish diffusion.
measurements: In situ STEM EDS mapping of surface composition vs. temperature
Particle size distribution evolution (number and diameter)
MD calculated surface energy gradients and diffusion fluxes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the observed rate of Au/Cu segregation and evaporation is negligible below 600 K, or if the segregation is uniform throughout the particle volume rather than surface-localized, or if the initial shape (icosahedral vs truncated octahedron) has no significant effect on the rate of reshaping, then the surface energy gradient hypothesis is falsified, and the sluggish diffusion/entropy stabilization hypothesis is supported.

Polymorphism, which describes the occurrence of different lattice structures in a crystalline material, is a critical phenomenon in materials science and condensed matter physics. Recently, configuration disorder was compositionally engineered into single lattices, leading to the discovery of high-entropy alloys and high-entropy oxides. For these novel entropy-stabilized forms of crystalline matter with extremely high structural stability, is polymorphism still possible? Here by employing in situ high-pressure synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction, we reveal a polymorphic transition from face-centred-cubic ( fcc ) structure to hexagonal-close-packing ( hcp ) structure in the prototype CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy. The transition is irreversible, and our in situ high-temperature synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction experiments at different pressures of the retained hcp high-entropy alloy reveal that the fcc phase is a stable polymorph at high temperatures, while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at lower temperatures. As pressure is increased, the critical temperature for the hcp -to- fcc transformation also rises.

The structural stability of the prototype CoCrFeMnNi HEA has been extensively studied in a wide temperature range from 55 K to its melting temperature of ∼1,600 K at ambient pressure [19] [31] [37] [38] but to our knowledge, no polymorphic transition has been observed. Conversely, high-pressure studies remain a virgin area in HEAs. In this work, using in situ high-pressure XRD techniques, we observed the first polymorphic transition from fcc to hcp in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA, as shown in Fig. 1c . Therefore, some critical questions are how and why can an hcp HEA form at high-pressure and can it be maintained at ambient conditions? According to the d -spacing of the main reflections of both fcc and hcp (that is, (111) and (220) of fcc , and (100), (002), (101) and (110) of hcp , as a function of pressure shown in Fig. 2a ), it is clear that the hcp -(002) and hcp -(110) planes inherit the fcc -(111) and fcc -(220) planes, respectively. In addition, Fig. 2b shows no obvious volume collapse during the transition; both the fcc and hcp phases seem to have almost the same volume per atom and bulk modulus. This is similar to many other fcc to hcp martensitic transitions, such as in cobalt [39]

High strength and ductility, often mutually exclusive properties of a structural material, are also responsible for damage tolerance. At low temperatures, due to high surface energy, single element metallic nanowires such as Ag usually transform into a more preferred phase via nucleation and propagation of partial dislocation through the nanowire, enabling superplasticity. In high entropy alloy (HEA) CoNiCrFeMn nanowires, the motion of the partial dislocation is hindered by the friction due to difference in the lattice parameter of the constituent atoms which is responsible for the hardening and lowering the ductility. In this study, we have examined the temperature-dependent superplasticity of single component Ag and multicomponent CoNiCrFeMn HEA nanowires using molecular dynamics simulations. The results demonstrate that Ag nanowires exhibit apparent temperature-dependent superplasticity at cryogenic temperature due to (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation behavior. Interestingly, HEA nanowires can perform exceptional strength-ductility trade-offs at cryogenic temperatures.
